0: In which country are the pyramids of Giza?
The Great Pyramid of Khufu is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing.
1: What title did the kings of ancient Egypt hold?
The word “pharaoh” comes from the Egyptian “per-aa”, meaning “great house”, in other words the palace.
2: Where in Greece were the ancient Olympic Games held?
According to tradition, the first Olympic Games took place in 776 BC.
3: In which country is the Great Wall?
Its earliest sections are more than 2,000 years old, but most of what you can see today dates from the Ming dynasty.
4: What were the fighters who battled in Roman arenas called?
The Colosseum in Rome could hold about 50,000 spectators who came to watch the gladiators.
5: What is the ancient Egyptian writing made of little pictures called?
Champollion managed to decipher them in 1822 thanks to the Rosetta Stone.
6: Which Carthaginian general crossed the Alps with elephants to attack Rome?
He crossed the Alps in 218 BC during the Second Punic War.
7: On which hill in Athens does the Parthenon stand?
The Parthenon, built in the 5th century BC, was dedicated to the goddess Athena.
8: Which king of Macedon conquered the Persian Empire all the way to India?
A pupil of the philosopher Aristotle, he founded many cities, including Alexandria in Egypt.
9: Which people of Mesopotamia invented cuneiform writing?
These wedge-shaped signs were pressed into clay tablets more than 5,000 years ago.
10: Which volcano buried the Roman city of Pompeii in 79 AD?
The ash preserved the city so well that you can still see its streets, frescoes and bakeries.
11: Which emperor unified China in 221 BC and was buried with an army made of clay?
His Terracotta Army has several thousand soldiers, each with a different face.
12: Which seafaring people created the alphabet that the Greek and Latin alphabets come from?
The Phoenicians came from the coast of what is now Lebanon and traded all over the Mediterranean.
13: Which king of Babylon is famous for his code of laws carved on a stone slab?
This basalt stele, about 3,750 years old, is now on display at the Louvre in Paris.
14: Which Scandinavian people sailed in longships?
The Vikings sailed as far as Iceland, Greenland and even North America.
15: What do we call the walled fortress where a medieval lord lived?
Many castles were protected by a moat and a drawbridge.
16: What were the noble sword-carrying warriors of old Japan called?
The samurai followed a code of honour called bushido, “the way of the warrior”.
17: Which Venetian merchant travelled to China, to the court of Kublai Khan?
The account of his journey, “The Travels of Marco Polo”, inspired generations of explorers.
18: Which leader founded the Mongol Empire, the largest connected land empire ever?
His real name was Temüjin; “Genghis Khan” is a title meaning “universal ruler”.
19: Which king of the Franks became emperor in the year 800?
His empire covered much of today’s France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and Italy.
20: Which ruler of the Mali Empire is famous for his enormous wealth in gold?
He appears on the Catalan Atlas of 1375 holding a gold nugget.
21: Which epidemic killed a huge part of Europe’s population in the mid-14th century?
Between 1347 and 1352, it killed between a third and a half of Europe’s population.
22: Which city was the capital of the Byzantine Empire?
This city on the Bosphorus is now called Istanbul.
23: Which English charter of 1215 limited the king’s powers for the first time?
King John was forced to seal it by his rebellious barons.
24: Which civilisation built the city of Chichén Itzá in Mexico?
Its great pyramid, El Castillo, has 365 steps in total, one for each day of the year.
25: In what year did William the Conqueror win the Battle of Hastings?
This conquest of England is told on the famous Bayeux Tapestry, nearly 70 metres long.
26: Which Viking explorer reached North America around the year 1000?
The remains of a Viking village were found at L’Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, Canada.
27: Which medieval city in southern Africa, with great stone walls, gave its name to a country?
“Zimbabwe” is thought to mean “houses of stone” in the Shona language.
28: Which explorer reached the Americas in 1492?
He thought he had reached the Indies, which is why the peoples of the Americas were called “Indians”.
29: Which artist painted the Mona Lisa?
Leonardo da Vinci was also an engineer and drew designs for flying machines.
30: Which French king, known as the Sun King, enlarged the Palace of Versailles?
His 72-year reign is one of the longest in European history.
31: What is the great artistic movement that began in Italy in the 15th century called?
The name comes from the idea of a “rebirth” of the art and learning of the ancient world.
32: In what year was the Bastille stormed in Paris?
14 July, the day the Bastille was stormed, became France’s national day.
33: What were the Spanish and Portuguese conquerors of the Americas called?
34: Which Portuguese navigator opened the sea route to India in 1498?
He sailed around Africa via the Cape of Good Hope to reach Calicut in India.
35: Which Spanish conquistador conquered the Inca Empire?
He captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa in 1532 with fewer than 200 men.
36: Which navigator led the first expedition around the world, setting off in 1519?
Magellan died on the way, in the Philippines; Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the last ship home in 1522.
37: In what year did the United States proclaim its Declaration of Independence?
It was adopted on 4 July, now the American national holiday.
38: Which Polish astronomer claimed that the Earth goes around the Sun?
His book on the movement of the heavenly bodies was published in 1543, the year he died.
39: Mexico City was built on the ruins of which Aztec city?
Tenochtitlan was built on an island in the middle of a lake, linked to land by causeways.
40: Which family of shoguns ruled Japan from 1603 to 1867?
During this period, Japan closed its borders to foreigners almost completely.
41: Which tsar founded the city of Saint Petersburg in 1703?
He travelled around Europe in disguise and even worked in a shipyard in the Netherlands.
42: Which French emperor was defeated at Waterloo in 1815?
The battle took place near Brussels, in Belgium; Napoleon was then exiled to the island of Saint Helena.
43: Who was the first man to walk on the Moon, in 1969?
He said: “That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.”
44: Which city was split in two by a wall that fell in 1989?
The Berlin Wall divided the city for 28 years, from 1961 to 1989.
45: In what year did the Second World War end?
In Europe the war ended on 8 May 1945, and in Asia on 2 September 1945.
46: Which Indian leader led the fight for India’s independence through non-violence?
He was nicknamed “Mahatma”, which means “great soul”.
47: Which ocean liner sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg?
It was said to be unsinkable; it went down on its very first voyage.
48: In what year did the First World War begin?
Belgium, a neutral country, was invaded as early as August 1914.
49: Which South African anti-apartheid activist spent 27 years in prison?
Released in 1990, he became South Africa’s first Black president in 1994.
50: Which US president led the North during the American Civil War?
He was assassinated in 1865, just days after the end of the war.
51: Who was the first person to travel into space, in 1961?
His flight around the Earth aboard Vostok 1 lasted about 108 minutes.
52: Which international organisation was created in 1945 to keep the peace?
The United Nations replaced the League of Nations, created after 1918.
53: Which era of rapid modernisation in Japan began in 1868?
Within a few decades, Japan had railways, factories and a modern army.
54: Which country was the first to give women the right to vote, in 1893?
Campaigner Kate Sheppard led this fight; her portrait is on the New Zealand 10-dollar note.
55: In what year was the Suez Canal opened?
This canal links the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea, so ships no longer need to sail around Africa.
56: Who invented movable-type printing in Europe around 1450?
Before him, books were copied by hand, which could take months.
57: In which country was paper invented?
Its invention is credited to Cai Lun around the year 105; the Egyptians wrote on papyrus.
58: Which brothers made the first powered aeroplane flight in 1903?
This first flight, in the United States, lasted only 12 seconds.
59: According to legend, his first words on the telephone were: “Mr Watson, come here, I want to see you.”
60: Which American inventor developed a long-lasting electric light bulb in 1879?
At the same time, the Englishman Joseph Swan was also working on an incandescent bulb.
61: Which instrument invented in China uses a magnetised needle to point north?
The compass let sailors find their way even when the sky was cloudy.
62: Which brothers showed the cinematograph to the public in 1895?
One of their first films showed a train arriving at La Ciotat station.
63: Which scientist discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic, in 1928?
He discovered it by chance, thanks to a mould that had grown in one of his culture dishes.
64: Which Italian scientist invented the electric battery in 1800?
The unit of electrical voltage, the volt, is named after him.
65: Which machine, improved by James Watt, launched the Industrial Revolution?
The unit of power, the watt, was named in his honour.
66: Which scientist carried out the first vaccination against rabies in 1885?
He saved a 9-year-old boy, Joseph Meister, who had been bitten by a rabid dog.
67: Who invented the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989?
The first website in history went online at CERN, near Geneva, in 1991.
68: Which Italian inventor, winner of the 1909 Nobel Prize, was a pioneer of radio?
In 1901, he managed to send a radio signal across the Atlantic Ocean.
69: Which German engineer patented one of the first petrol-powered cars in 1886?
In 1888, his wife Bertha Benz made the first long-distance car journey, about 100 km.
